full_judgment:
5. It was the case of the writ-respondent Nos. 6-9 that after cancellation of the lease of the writ- petitioners (respondent Nos. 1-4 herein) on May 29, 1994 the case plot was allotted to respondent Nos. 7 and 8 (writ-respondent Nos. 3 and 4) on June 6, 1994. The writ-respondent Nos. 3 and 4 executed a power of attorney in favour of the writ-respondent No.5 (respondent No.9 in appeal No. 155 of 2000), for the management and disposal of the property and the said respondent upon obtaining permission for sale on February 12, 1996 from the authority while proposed to sell the case plot, the writ-respondent Nos. 6-9 purchased the same on April 21, 1996 by a registered deed of sale without knowing about filing and pendency of the Writ Petition No. 2127 of 1994. It is the contention of the writ-respondent Nos. 6.9 that they are the bonafide purchasers of the plot with due consideration without knowledge of the pendency of the Rule. 

 6. The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 154 of 2000 opposed the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition stating that lease in favour of the respondent Nos. 1-4 was executed on July 30, 1980 and according to terms of clause 3 of the said lease deed, the said respondents were required to make construction within 3 years from the date of commencement of the lease and failing which the lease agreement as per clause 23 was liable to be cancelled and as the respondents did not make any construction within the period of 9 years from the date of commencement of the lease they were served with show cause notice on September 16, 1989 and the respondents prayed for 6 months' extension of time on October 11, 1989 and though time was extended till June 30, 1990 the respondents did not make any construction and thereupon, again show cause notice was served upon the respondents on September 2, 1990 and the respondents again prayed for extension of time till June 30, 1991, but as respondents neither started construction nor prayed for any further extension of time, as such, on May 29, 1994 the lease was validly cancelled and the respondents were duly informed. The writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 asserted that the alleged letter dated 14-10-1993 allegedly seeking extension of time upto 31-12-1994 was manufactured and the writ-respondent No.2 did not receive the said letter. It was also the case of the writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that after cancellation of lease of the plot in question the same has been allotted to the writ respondent Nos. 3 and 4 (respondent Nos. 5 and 6 in Appeal No. 154 of 2000) and lease deed has been executed on September 14, 1994 and possession has been made over to the fresh allottees on 27-8-1994. It was also asserted by the writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that names of the fresh allottees have been mutated in respect of the case plot, that the fresh allottees executed a power of attorney in favour of writ-respondent No.5 to do all acts touching the plot on their behalf and an application was filed for permission to work through the said attorney and permission was given on 23-8-1994, that writ- respondent No.5 constructed building according to the approved plan and he brought electricity, water and sewerage connections to the case plot in his name, that writ-respondent No.5 on behalf of the writ-respondent Nos. 3 and 4 proposed to sell the property to respondent Nos. 6-9 and after obtaining permission on February 12, 1996 sold the property to respondent Nos. 6-9 on April 21, 1996 and the writ-respondent Nos. 3 and 4 handed over possession of the plot to the writ-respondent Nos. 6- 9 on April 21, 1996, that after purchase the writ- respondent Nos. 6-9 applied for mutation of their names but their names were not mutated because of the pendency of the writ petition, that writ- petitioners were never in physical possession of the plot in question nor raised any boundary wall. 

 7. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute primarily on the finding that the cancellation of the lease of the writ-petitioners and the allotment of the plot to the writ-respondent Nos. 3 and 4 were malafide. While making the Rule absolute the High Court Division observed that no paper was placed from the side of the writ-respondent No. 1 to show that decision for allotment was taken on October 25, 1993 as seen from the letter of allotment dated 6-6-1994 (Annexure J to the writ petition) and also observed subsequent to the show cause notice dated 2-9-1990 no other show cause was issued and the Government did not consider the prayer for extension of time made by the writ-petitioners on 26-11-1990 "which the Government received in due course" and there was no material on the record that writ-petitioners lease was cancelled on the basis of the show cause notice dated 2-9-1990 and "in the circumstances it is too hard to believe that the decision for cancellation of the lease has been made on the basis of the show cause notice dated 2-9-90, against which reply was given long before the cancellation, which deserved consideration from the authority inasmuch as the right to lease property is a valuable right, particularly being a right to perpetual lease, which is inheritable in nature." The High Court Division further observed "and now while comparing the left thumb impressions of respondent Nos. 3 and 4 as appearing in the applications made for allotment of plots in 1994 with those appearing in Annexure-Q it seems that those are not similar and of the same persons and are different detectable to the naked eye". The High Court Division also observed "it appears that the impugned cancellation has been made in the year 1994 after expiry of 4 years of the issuance of the show cause notice dated 2-9-90 and without considering the petitioners reply dated 26-11-90 to the said show cause notice dated 2-9-90 though received by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and that as it cannot be said that order of cancellation was passed on the basis of the show cause notice dated 2-9-90, "and in the circumstance is all fairness the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 ought to have issued a fresh show cause notice upon the petitioners as contemplated by Clause 23 of the lease deed prior to the issuance of the letter of  cancellation on 25-5-94" (sic) (in fact, allotment was cancelled on 29-5-1994) and petitioners were "entitled to a reply from the Government on either prayer for extension of time, either accepting or rejecting, and that the Government cannot sit over such prayer, moreso when the right of the citizen is in danger". The High Court Division also observed that allotment to the writ-respondent Nos. 3 and 4 was made treating them as affected persons, "but the materials on record of the case revealed that particular plots were earmarked for the affected persons and the plot in question is not such a plot but is a regular plot for which the affected persons are not entitled and accordingly, the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 are not entitled to get allotment of the demised plot". The High Court Division has further observed that the allotment to the writ-respondent Nos. 3. and 4 was made contrary to the policy of the Government since the kind of the land allotted to the writ petitioners as per policy was to be allotted to a group consisting of 4/6 persons but upon cancellation of the lease of the writ-petitioners the same has been allotted to 2 persons. It has further been observed by the High Court Division that although from Annexure-J to the writ petition it appears that the decision for allotment in favour of respondent Nos. 1 and 4 was taken as far back as on 25-10-93 whereas cancellation of the lease was made only on 29-5-94 and the applications for allotment by the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 were made in the year 1994. The High Court Division further observed that "there are other plots lying vacant till date allotted to persons similarly placed with the petitioners and against them no action has been taken by the respondents" and that the writ- respondent Nos. 1 and 2 could not rebut the claim of the writ-petitioners that their possession of the demised plot was not taken from them. The High Court Division finally observed, "we are of the opinion that the actions of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 lack fairness and therefore, the lease deed as cancelled is malafide and the impugned cancellation is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the subsequent allotment in favour of respondent Nos. 3 and 4 was not legal and valid". 

 9. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that admittedly the writ-petitioners having not made any construction on the case plot and thereby violated the provision of clause 3 of the lease deed, the lease of the writ-petitioners was liable to be cancelled for which notice dated 2-9-1990 was served and thereupon the lease was cancelled on 29-5-1994 and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in making the Rule absolute upon observing since cancellation was made after expiry of 4 years Government ought to have issued fresh show cause notice, that once a lease is liable to be cancelled there is no further requirement that the order of cancellation has to be passed within a certain period of time and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in finding the order of cancellation of lease on 29-5-1994 illegal simply because the show cause notice was issued on 2-9-1990, particularly when there is no assertion in the writ petition that the writ-petitioners changed their position by making construction or otherwise between the date of issuance of the show cause notice and the date of cancellation of the lease, that the High Court Division failed to appreciate properly the decision of Moni Begum vs RAJUK, 46 DLR (AD) 154 and wrongly held that in writ jurisdiction review application is not maintainable, that new relevant facts having bearing on the case having been discovered and a review having been sought on that ground, the High Court Division was wrong in summarily dismissing the review application without applying its judicial mind to the new evidence placed before it. 

 10. The learned Counsels appearing for the appellants in Appeal Nos. 152 and 155 have submitted that the proceeding initiated upon a writ petition before the constitution Bench of the High Court Division is undoubtedly being civil proceeding and there being nothing in Article 102(2) of the Constitution to preclude the High Court Division from exercising the power of review which inheres in every court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent miscarriage of justice or to correct grave and palpable errors committed by it, the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the review application holding the same not maintainable and it has also been submitted that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the decision reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 and thereupon wrongly held that in writ jurisdiction review application is not maintaihable. 

 11. In the case of Moni Begum vs Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakha this Division while considering the question of application of the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the proceedings in writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution observed that the provision of section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure "does not in terms apply to proceedings in writ in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. But the Court in its discretion can apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience. In what situations the principles of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applied and to what extent may perhaps be left to the wise discretion of the Court itself. In other words, barring what is specifically provided for in the Rules themselves, the Court is the master of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience." In the said case Mr Latifur Rahman, J, (as he then was) has observed that the Writ Court being a civil Court though does not possess specifically powers as are in Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Writ Court must possess this power of doing justice in a case and whether Court will exercise such power is a matter of judicial discretion for that Court. 

 13. In support of the said submission the learned Counsel has referred to a decision in the case of Hussain Bakhsh vs Settlement Commissioner and another reported in 21 DLR (SC) 456 wherein it has been observed, "A review of such an order is therefore, competent under clause (b) of section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure". A review under section 114(b) CPC lies in case of decree or order from which no appeal was allowed by the CPC. In the background of the decision referred to above it has been submitted by the learned Counsel that it is not correct that review is at all available before the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Khadomul Islam Chowdhury vs Bangladesh and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 111 wherein it has been observed "the question involved, no doubt, is of great public importance, but none of the Counsels appearing for the parties challenged the power of the High Court Division to review its order made under Article 102 of the Constitution". The fact of the aforesaid case is that a writ petition was heard in the absence of one of the respondents and the Rule was made absolute. Thereupon, respondent in whose absence the writ petition was disposed of filed an application before the same very Bench with the prayer for re-hearing of the writ petition and the High Court Division allowed the same and restored the writ petition to its file and number. As against the order of the High Court Division restoring the writ petition for fresh hearing the appeal was filed. The learned Counsel in support of his contention since there is nothing in Article 102 precluding the High Court Division from reviewing its order and, as such, the said Division in the exigency of a case or to correct palpable error as well as to prevent miscarriage of justice is very much competent to exercise power of review in writ jurisdiction has referred to the case of Ariban Tuleshwar Sharma vs Ariban Pishak Sharma and others reported in AIR 1979 SC 1047 wherein it has been observed "It is true as observed by this Court in Shivdeo Singh vs State of Punjab (AIR 1963 SC 1909) there is nothing in Article 226 of the Constitution to preclude a High Court from exercising the power of review which inheres in every Court of plenary jurisdiction to prevent miscarriage of justice or to correct grave and palpable errors committed by it. But, there are definitive limits to the exercise of the power of review. The power of review may be exercised on the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of the person seeking the review or could not be produced by him at the time when the order was made; it may be exercised where some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record is found; it may also be exercised on any analogous ground. But it may not be exercised on the ground that the decision was erroneous on merits. That would be the province of a Court of appeal". The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of State of Kerala vs PK Syed Akbar Sahib, reported in AIR 1988 SC 702 wherein it has been observed "in our considered opinion the High Court should have entertained the application for review". It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division in Review Petition Nos. 10 and 11, as against which Civil Appeal Nos. 152 and 153 have been filed, the said Division has placed reliance in holding that review application in writ jurisdiction is not maintainable on the decision in the case of Azra Zaman Chowdhury vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 34 DLR 247 wherein it has been observed "that the High Court Division is not empowered under the Constitution of Bangladesh or under any other law to review its judgment made in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution". The High Court Division held the same on the view that in a proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution, there is no provision either in the Constitution itself or in any other law providing for any such review of any judgment passed by the High Court Division in exercising its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution and also, upon referring to Article 105 of the Constitution, has observed that the provision of the said Article empowered the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court to review any judgment pronounced by it and such specific power of reviewing its judgment or order is conspicuously absent so far as the High Court Division is concerned. The High Court Division has also referred to the case of Omar Faruk (Md) and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 51 DLR 118 (same has also been reported in 1999 BLD 70 wherein it has been observed that the jurisdiction is the creation of the statute and as the Constitution is silent as to power of the High Court Division to review its judgment and order passed in writ jurisdiction there is no scope for entertaining the application for review and to review the judgment or order passed by the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction. The view expressed in the case reported 21 DLR (SC) 456 and 46 DLR (AD) 154 as to power to the High Court Division to exercise the power of review and as to application of the provision as in sections 114 and 141 of the Civil Procedure Code has already been quoted hereinabove. 

 14. The learned Counsel for the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 152 of 2000 has submitted that the Court exercises its power, either in the writ jurisdiction or in the ordinary civil jurisdiction, for dispensation of justice and in doing so the Court is competent to exercise its discretion in the background of the materials brought before it in one form or other or, in other words, while seeks exercise of discretion either by way of review or re-hearing or reconsideration of its judgment earlier made in the background of the fresh material(s) brought before it. The learned Counsel has also submitted that in Moni Begum's case this Division has in no way precluded the High Court Division from exercising its discretion either recoursing to review, or re-hearing to revise the decision already made in a case upon placement of the materials which earlier could not be placed after due diligence before it and if the same would have been placed before the Writ Court the judgment already delivered would not have been one made, but would have been otherwise. In the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 154 this Division has observed that High Court Division in its discretion can "apply the principles as distinguished from the technical provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to meet  the exigencies of the situation in appropriate cases on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience." It is true in the Constitution there is no provision empowering the High Court Division to review its judgment and order, but it is also true that there was no provision precluding the High Court Division from exercising power of review. The Court's inherent power to do justice to the parties before it is an accepted one and for that the form in which the Court shall dispense justice is a matter for the Court or, in other words, it may either by way of review of its judgment or upon revising its judgment in the background of the material(s) brought before it subsequent to the pronouncement of the judgment since "the Court is the master of its own procedure and it will exercise both its procedural and substantive discretions only on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience." 

 16. There being no dispute that the Court is for dispensation of justice and in doing so is competent to exercise its discretion to advance the cause of justice upon resorting to the procedure that would advance the cause of justice, equity and good conscience and as there is nothing in Article 102 of the Constitution to preclude the High Court Division from exercising the power of review we are of the view that the High Court Division is very much competent to entertain an application for review and to revise its judgment if a case for review is made out or, in other words, the material(s), which if would have been before the Court the judgment already made would not have been the one but different is placed before the High Court Division then the said Division to advance cause of action is not precluded from reviewing its judgment. 

 18. The learned Counsels for the appellants have submitted that the respondent Nos. 1-4 did not make out any case of malafide or non-transparency as regard cancellation of their allotment of the plot in question and allotment of the said plot to the appellants in appeal No. 155 of 2000 (the writ respondent Nos. 6-9). The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-4 has submitted that the elements highlighting malafide are very much on record and the said elements are primarily, the decision to cancel the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 was taken in hot haste. In elaborating the same he has submitted that the allotment was cancelled on the very day on which notings were made for the purpose of taking decision as regard cancellation of the plot allotted to the respondent Nos. 1-4 and that policy decision that was taken in the meeting held on 25-10-93 was in respect of all the affected persons and the policy decision so taken though was of generai nature but allotment was made only to 2 affected persons from amongst the affected persons and the decision to cancel allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 was taken after lapse of more or less 4 years from the date of service of 2nd show cause notice. 

 19. In refutal of the aforesaid contentions of the respondents it has been submitted by the learned Counsels for the appellants that materials on record, particularly from the decision No.2 of the meeting held on 28-2-94, it would clearly be seen what prompted the authority to make the allotment in question avoiding procrastination. It is seen from the materials on record that the matter of allotment of plot to the affected persons was pending for sufficiently long time and thereupon there was agitation by the affected person for finalisation of allotment of plot to the affected person without further procrastination. The learned Counsel for the respondents heavily relied on the fact that matter of cancellation of the plot allotted to the respondent Nos. 1-4 was taken in the course of the day although 2nd notice for cancellation was issued about 4 years back. We have already observed that there are materials on the record that prompted the authority to take decision relating to the matter of cancellation of the allotment without sitting over the same any further. The learned Counsel for the appellants in appeal No. 155 of 2000 has submitted that merely for the delay in taking decision in a matter no bad motive can be ascribed to the decision taken and, in that respect, has referred to the observation made in the case of Chairman, BCSIR vs Abdul Khaleque reported in 43 DLR 209, and, as such, the learned Counsel submitted conversely, in view of the materials on record, bad motive cannot be ascribed to the decision taken by the authority for the cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 avoiding procrastination. 

 20. The contention of mala fide either on the ground of delay in taking decision or for taking decision avoiding procrastination in a given case is to be considered in the context of facts and circumstances of the same as well as on consideration of the tangible material(s) in the background whereof reasonable deduction can be made or conclusion can be arrived at as regard contention of malafide. 

 25. The High Court Division while holding that in canceling the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 there was discrimination or, in other words, they were not treated at par with the other allottee i.e. allottees similar to the category of the respondents, in that their allotments were not cancelled. The High Court Division in this respect was very much in error in that materials on record show that allotment of other allottees similarly placed to the position of respondent Nos. 1-4 were cancelled. The High Court Division in view of the materials on record was also in error in holding that although in the letter of allotment it was mentioned decision for making allotment to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 was taken on 25-10-93 but there was no such decision in the file placed before it by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, ie appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154 of 2000, on being directed by the said Division in that it was in the allotment letter that allotment to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 was made in pursuant to the decision taken in the meeting of the Allotment Committee held on 25-10-93 as because the said respondents were the affected persons and they were listed as affected persons in the list that was made final in the meeting held on 25-10-93. It may be mentioned decision was made on 29-5-1994 for making allotment to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 and thereupon allotment letter was issued to the said respondents on June 6, 1994. The High Court Division. in declaring the order of cancellation to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the order of cancellation as  malafide and the same to have been passed without jurisdiction and the subsequent actions had no legal validity, held that the order of cancellation was not made on the basis of 2nd show cause notice. The file upon looking into which the High Court Division took the aforesaid view was also fi led before us and therefrom it is seen, in fact, decision was taken in the background of the show cause notices issued on three occasions. Although the respondent Nos. 1 to 4 tried to make out a case that they on October 14, 1993 filed an application addressed to Assistant Commissioner, Settlement, Directorate of Housing seeking extension of time up to December 31, 1994 and the same as was not replied to in the negative they were in genuine belief that time was extended to the date prayed for. The writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 denied addressing any such letter to the writ-respondent No. 2 and receiving of the same. The respondent Nos. 1-4 in the background of the said denial by the writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 has not placed any reliable material before the Court to establish the fact of receiving of the letter dated 14-10-93 by the authority. 

 27. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the respondents that in the letter of cancellation there is no mention that respondent Nos. 1-4's allotment was cancelled after serving show cause notice and, as such, the same was not a letter of cancellation as per law. In the letter of cancellation it has been mentioned that the lease of the respondent Nos. 1-4 has been cancelled pursuant to the provision of Clause 23 of the lease deed for violation of clause 3 of the leased deed. The undenied  position is that show cause notice, in all 3 (three), of which receipt of first and second admitted but disputed receipt of the 3rd show cause notice, and in all the show cause notices the respondent Nos. 1-4 were asked to show cause why their lease shall not be cancelled as per provision of clause 23 of the lease deed for violation of clause 3 of the lease deed. So, the submissions  so made is not well founded and merited. It has also been submitted on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that cancellation of their allotment lacked transparency as well as there was absence of fairness on the part of the authority in cancelling their allotment. As it appears contention of lack of transparency has been made in the background of the fact that the 2nd show cause notice was issued on September 2, 1990 and on receipt whereof respondents prayed for extension of time up to June 30, 1991 and thereafter allotment was cancelled on May 29, 1994 and the letter of cancellation was issued on that very date. In our view of being somewhat late in taking decision as well as in the communication of decision as regard cancellation of allotment for violation of condition in the lease deed, in all cases, as is the instant case, cannot be considered lacks transparency. In the facts and circumstances of each individual case matter of transparency in decision making and communication thereof is to be considered. The contention of absence of fairness in the background of the facts and circumstances of the matter is also not well merited. It was also the contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that as the authority did not reply to their prayer for extension of time till June 30, 1991 and thereafter, as no action was taken they were definite as they had got the plan approved from the RAJUK for making construction and had taken steps for making construction the authority has dropped the matter of cancellation of their allotment after lapse of so many years since September 1990, but suddenly, the authority initiated the proposal for cancellation in May 1994 and made the decision final for cancellation in the course of a day and the said hot-haste step clearly shows lack of fairness. It is seen from the file, which was produced before the High Court Division also, that 3 show cause notices were issued to the respondent Nos. 1-4 of which the said respondents disputed receipt of the last one, and also made the allegation that the same was manufactured for the purpose of filing review before the High Court Division. Since respondents' allotment has been cancelled after serving show cause notices and because of undisputed position no construction was made as required by the terms of lease deed within the specified time as well as within the extended period, absence of fairness can hardly be attributed to the action of cancellation of allotment of the respondents. The allegation of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that the fact of issuance of 3rd show cause notice is a manufactured one, in ourview, in the background of the materials placed by the authority, said allegation to have been made without any basis as well as the same has been made for allegation's sake and we are of the view that the allegation so made as against the issuance of the 3rd show cause notice is not well founded and the said allegation has been made to cover up the lapse on the part of respondents in making construction in the plot so cancelled as per provision of their lease deed. It is difficult to accept the contention of the respondent Nos. 1-4 that there was absence of fairness on the part of the authority in cancelling their allotment since issuance of the 2nd show cause notice and giving reply thereof by them there was lapse of sufficient period, which the respondents contended sufficiently long, and only in May 1994 proposal was initiated for cancellation and was made final in one day and thereupon the letter of cancellation was issued on that very date as, in our view, prompt decision in the background of the materials on record taken cannot be considered to have lacked fairness or transparency on the part of the authority since first, there is no time limit for taking decision for cancelling allotment like the one as of the respondent Nos. 1-4 within a specified time after issuance of the show cause notice, second, the authority was not precluded from taking decision in the light of the show cause notice issued to the respondent Nos. 1-4 after lapse of 3 years and a little more time. In view of our discussions made hereinabove we are of the view the action of the Writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 i.e. appellants in Civil Appeal Nos. 153 and 154 of 2000, in the matter of cancellation of the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 cannot be considered malafide or, in other words, it can also be not said that the action of the said authority lacked fairness and transparency and, as such, the High Court Division was in error in holding that the action of the Writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in cancelling the allotment of the respondent Nos. 1-4 and making allotment of the said land to the respondent Nos. 7 and 8 was not legally valid and was made without lawful authority. 

 28. In our view, High Court Division was in error in rejecting the application filed by the Writ-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as well as by the Writ respondent Nos. 6-9 seeking review of its judgment since the Court is for dispensation of justice and in doing so the Court is competent to exercise its discretion in a case where party seeking review/reconsideration of the judgment of a particular Court upon placing material(s), which if would have been before the Court, the same would have not been the one the Court has made and, in such a situation, the Court for dispensation of justice is quite competent to recourse to a procedure, of which the same is the master, to advance the cause of justice as wel1 as on the ground of equity and good conscience. The procedure that the Court is quite competent to recourse may either be by review or some other suitable procedure. Moreover, provision of Article 102(2) or any other provision of the Constitution do not preclude the High Court Division either to reconsider or to review or to see the correctness or its judgment earlier made on furnishing of fresh material(s) by a party to the case which, according to him, if were before the Court the judgment would have been otherwise than the one made.
